desc:
nums is a permutation of the integers 0..n-1. Two kinds of inversions are counted:

  • a global inversion is any pair i < j with nums[i] > nums[j];
  • a local inversion is a global inversion whose indices are neighbours, that is j = i + 1.

Every local inversion is also a global one. Return true if the number of global inversions is exactly equal to the number of local inversions, otherwise false.

nums = [1, 0, 2]   global 1, local 1  -> true
nums = [1, 2, 0]   global 2, local 1  -> false
hints: Counting both kinds of inversions directly takes O(n<sup>2</sup>) for the global one. But you do not need the counts: the two numbers are equal exactly when there is no non-local inversion at all.
A non-local inversion is a pair i < j with j ≥ i + 2 and nums[i] > nums[j]. Ask what the array must look like if no such pair exists.
In a permutation of 0..n-1, a value that sits 2 or more places away from its own index forces a non-local inversion. So check abs(nums[i] - i) ≤ 1 for every index.
editorial: Global inversions are a superset of local ones, so the counts are equal if and only if every global inversion is local. We therefore only have to decide whether some pair i < j, j - i ≥ 2, has nums[i] > nums[j].

Claim: such a pair exists exactly when some value is at distance 2 or more from its home index. If nums[i] ≥ i + 2, then among the n - i - 1 positions after i there are only n - 1 - nums[i] values larger than nums[i] (at most n - i - 3), so at least two of the later positions hold smaller values, and one of them is non-adjacent to i. Symmetrically for nums[i] ≤ i - 2. Conversely, if every value is within 1 of its index, a non-local inversion would need a value to move at least 2 places. So one pass testing abs(nums[i] - i) ≤ 1 is enough: O(n) time and O(1) space.
A running-maximum version is equivalent: keep the maximum of nums[0..i-2] and fail as soon as it exceeds nums[i].
